# Why the girl in the white T-shirt suddenly raises her hand above her head

## Where this happens in the video

The clip is archival footage titled "San Pablo City Public Market, December 23, 2006"
(The San Pablo City Archive Project, created by Gerry Alanguilan). The relevant shot
is the hand-held walk-along sequence down the crowded market **sidewalk**, which runs
from roughly **2:03 to 3:00**. The camera drifts forward with the shoppers past a row
of vendor stalls shaded by yellow-and-green market umbrellas, with fruit stalls and
small wooden display carts crowding the edge of the pavement.

The specific action happens at about **2:10–2:14** (≈130–134 s). The girl in question
wears a **white/light T-shirt and black track pants with a white side stripe**; the
companion beside her is the woman in the **green cardigan, blue-striped headband and
pale yellow/khaki trousers**. They are shuffling along in an almost stationary,
jammed crowd (the camera barely advances during these four seconds).

## What she actually does

She abruptly shoots her right arm straight up over her head, and then **keeps it up
for about four seconds** before letting it drop and walking on.

## The reason for the sudden action

**She is pushing an obstacle out of her way — a big sheet of translucent plastic that
hangs down into the walkway at head height.**

One of the vendors has a small wooden display cart parked right at the edge of the
sidewalk (its rack is hung with small goods, with a red-and-white box on the table).
To protect the merchandise from rain and dust, the vendor has draped a large
white/clear plastic tarpaulin sheet over the cart, slung up to the frame of the
yellow market umbrella. Because the sidewalk is extremely narrow and packed with
Christmas shoppers, that plastic sheet droops out over the only gap people can walk
through, hanging at about head/face height.

So the raised hand is a purely practical gesture: she reaches up, grabs and **lifts
the drooping plastic sheet clear of her head and hair, holds it up while she squeezes
past the cart, and lets it fall back down behind her.** Because the crowd is at a
near standstill at that moment, she has to stand there holding it aloft for several
seconds, which is why the arm stays up — and while she holds it, the two women
walking directly behind her (one in a black top, one in a white T-shirt) duck through
the gap she is holding open, so she is effectively keeping the sheet up for her group
as well as herself.

## Why this reading is certain

It is not a wave, not a greeting, not a signal to anyone, not hailing a jeepney, and
not reaching for merchandise. The give-away is that **person after person does exactly
the same thing at exactly the same spot**: watching the sequence frame by frame, a man
in a black long-sleeved shirt and cap lifts the same sheet just before her (≈2:09),
she lifts it from ≈2:10 to ≈2:14, and afterwards a steady stream of other shoppers
repeats the identical arm-above-the-head movement at that cart and at other similarly
covered carts further along the same sidewalk (e.g. ≈2:05–2:08, ≈2:22–2:30, and again
around ≈2:43–2:50 and ≈2:50–3:00). A one-off gesture by one girl could be ambiguous;
an entire queue of unrelated pedestrians performing it at the same physical point
shows it is the standard way to get past the low-hanging plastic stall covers on this
sidewalk.

## Short answer

Because a vendor's translucent plastic rain/dust cover, draped over a display cart and
hung from the market umbrella, hangs down across the narrow sidewalk at head height.
She throws her hand up to shove the plastic sheet up and out of the way so it does not
hit her head and face, holds it raised while the jammed crowd inches past, and lets it
drop once she and the people with her are through.
